claims.evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis based on the authors' understanding of embryonic development.

claims.claim: The authors generated yolk sac-like cells (YSLCs) by simultaneously stimulating ACTIVIN-A, WNT, and JAK/STAT signalling in peri-implantation-like human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs).
claims.source: To do this, we first generated yolk sac-like cells (YSLCs) by simultaneously stimulating ACTIVIN-A, WNT, and JAK/STAT signalling in peri-implantation-like human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) (Gafni et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach taken by the authors, with a citation to Gafni et al., 2013 for the hPSC type used.

claims.claim: YSLCs induce the expression of pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers at the expense of mesoderm and endoderm markers in hESCs by inhibiting BMP and WNT signalling pathways.
claims.source: We then modelled the interaction between these YSLCs and hESCs, which revealed that YSLCs induce the expression of pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers at the expense of mesoderm and endoderm markers in hESCs by inhibiting BMP and WNT signalling pathways.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes the main experimental findings of the study.

claims.claim: Conventionally, hESCs have been used as a reliable model of the human epiblast, harbouring a post-implantation, 'primed' pluripotent state.
claims.source: Conventionally, hESCs have been used as a reliable model of the human epiblast, harbouring a post-implantation, 'primed' pluripotent state (Nakamura et al., 2016; Shao et al., 2017a; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2016; Shao et al., 2017a; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Human extended pluripotent stem cells (hEPSCs) were shown to have extra-embryonic potential when incorporated into mouse embryos.
claims.source: We hypothesised that human extended pluripotent stem cells (hEPSCs) were an appropriate candidate as they were shown to have extra-embryonic potential when incorporated into mouse embryos (Yang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The combination of WNT (via the GSK3 activator CHIR 99021) and ACTIVIN-A pathway activation led to the greatest upregulation of SOX17 at the expense of SOX2 after 6 days in hEPSCs.
claims.source: By analysing SOX17 and SOX2 reporter fluorescence intensity, we discerned that the combination of WNT (via the GSK3 activator CHIR 99021) and ACTIVIN-A pathway activation led to the greatest upregulation of SOX17 at the expense of SOX2 after 6 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: ACTIVIN-A and WNT signalling are involved in the specification of mouse, monkey, and human primitive endoderm in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: This result is in line with ACTIVIN-A and WNT signalling being involved in the specification of mouse, monkey, and human primitive endoderm in vitro and in vivo (Anderson et al., 2017; Blakeley et al., 2015; Boroviak et al., 2015; Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2017; Blakeley et al., 2015; Boroviak et al., 2015; Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Human leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) is necessary for proliferation during the conversion of hEPSCs to YSLCs.
claims.source: We further optimised the medium by increasing the concentrations of both CHIR 99021 and ACTIVIN-A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), and removing the other cytokines from the LCDM medium apart from human leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), which we found to be necessary for proliferation during the conversion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: ACL treatment on hEPSCs results in a strong shift from a SOX2 high, SOX17 low population of cells to the converse.
claims.source: To further assess the effect of ACL treatment on hEPSCs after 6 days of culture, we analysed the expression levels of SOX17 and SOX2 using reporter fluorescence at the single cell level. This revealed a strong shift from an originally SOX2 high, SOX17 low population of cells, to the converse (Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C.

claims.claim: Pan-endodermal markers SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES were all upregulated following ACL treatment in hEPSCs.
claims.source: Furthermore, gene expression analysis showed that pan-endodermal markers SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES were all upregulated following ACL treatment (Figure 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Despite observed downregulation of SOX2 expression, the expression of OCT4 and NANOG increased following ACL treatment in hEPSCs.
claims.source: Despite observed downregulation of SOX2 expression, the expression of OCT4 and NANOG increased (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which has previously been observed in hESCs overexpressing SOX17 (Séguin et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, and a citation to Séguin et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The upregulation of OCT4 and NANOG despite SOX2 downregulation has previously been observed in hESCs overexpressing SOX17.
claims.source: Despite observed downregulation of SOX2 expression, the expression of OCT4 and NANOG increased (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which has previously been observed in hESCs overexpressing SOX17 (Séguin et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Séguin et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The inability of ACL to fully downregulate pluripotency markers in hPSCs may indicate that cells may still preserve some features of pluripotent cells.
claims.source: The inability of ACL to fully downregulate pluripotency markers in hPSCs may indicate that cells may still preserve some features of pluripotent cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is presented as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Rset hPSCs harbour a pluripotent state that is intermediate between pre-implantation 'ground-state' naïve pluripotency and post-implantation lineage-biased primed pluripotency.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gafni et al., 2013 and Kilens et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Conventional primed RUES2-GLR hESCs are similar to the post-implantation human epiblast.
claims.source: To determine whether ACL could also induce endodermal fate in other hPSCs, we treated both RUES2-GLR Rset hPSCs, which harbour a pluripotent state that is intermediate between pre-implantation 'ground-state' naïve pluripotency and post-implantation lineage-biased primed pluripotency (Gafni et al., 2013; Kilens et al., 2018), and conventional primed RUES2-GLR hESCs, that are similar to the post-implantation human epiblast (Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molè et al., 2021 and Nakamura et al., 2016.

claims.claim: After 6 days of ACL treatment, endodermal markers were upregulated and SOX2 was downregulated in both Rset hPSCs and hESCs.
claims.source: After 6 days of treatment, endodermal markers were upregulated and SOX2 was downregulated in both Rset hPSCs and hESCs (Figure 1E–K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E–K.

claims.claim: The expression pattern of upregulated endodermal markers and downregulated SOX2 was also observed after 1 month of culture in ACL.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on human embryo development from fertilization through implantation and early post-implantation stages, describing blastocyst formation, lineage specification (epiblast, hypoblast, trophoblast), implantation timing, amniotic cavity formation, and gastrulation onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 are all supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Edwards et al., 1970; Steptoe et al., 1971; Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018; Deglincerti et al., 2016; Shahbazi et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2016; Shahbazi, 2020). These represent well-established background knowledge about human embryo development and serve as context for the study.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that the mouse AVE secretes signaling inhibitors to pattern the embryo, that AVE-like cells have been identified in primate embryos, that human embryos can be cultured to 14 days in vitro, that hESCs have been used to model embryogenesis, but that current stem cell models lack extra-embryonic tissues which are likely key regulators of human epiblast patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 are supported by appropriate citations to established literature. Claim C19 is an observational statement about the field that is accurate. Claim C20 is presented as a hypothesis/motivation for the study and is reasonable given the known role of extra-embryonic tissues in mouse development. Together these claims establish the rationale for the study.

results.result: The authors generated yolk sac-like cells (YSLCs) by stimulating ACTIVIN-A, WNT, and JAK/STAT signaling in peri-implantation-like hPSCs, and these YSLCs induce pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers in hESCs while suppressing mesoderm and endoderm markers through BMP and WNT pathway inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 represent the core findings of the manuscript and are supported by extensive experimental data presented in Figures 1-7. The generation of YSLCs is documented through marker expression analysis, and their effects on hESCs are demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches including conditioned medium experiments, signaling pathway analysis, and marker expression studies.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that hESCs are conventionally used as models of the primed post-implantation epiblast, and that hEPSCs have extra-embryonic potential when incorporated into mouse embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by appropriate citations (Nakamura et al., 2016; Shao et al., 2017a; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019 for C23; Yang et al., 2017 for C24). These establish the rationale for cell line selection in the study.

results.result: Through a screen of signaling pathway activators, the authors identified that combined WNT (CHIR 99021) and ACTIVIN-A activation led to the greatest SOX17 upregulation at the expense of SOX2 in hEPSCs after 6 days, consistent with known roles of these pathways in primitive endoderm specification, and that LIF is necessary for proliferation during conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F. The screen methodology is clearly described, results are quantified, and the findings are consistent with cited literature on primitive endoderm specification (Anderson et al., 2017; Blakeley et al., 2015; Boroviak et al., 2015; Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019).

results.result: ACL treatment of hEPSCs results in a shift from SOX2-high/SOX17-low to SOX17-high/SOX2-low cells, with upregulation of pan-endodermal markers (SOX17, GATA6, EOMES) and increased OCT4/NANOG expression despite SOX2 downregulation, suggesting cells may preserve some pluripotent features.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1A-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, including both single-cell fluorescence analysis and gene expression measurements. Claim C31 is supported by citation to Séguin et al., 2008. Claim C32 is a reasonable interpretation of the data showing incomplete downregulation of pluripotency markers.

results.result: ACL treatment induces endodermal marker upregulation and SOX2 downregulation in both Rset hPSCs (intermediate pluripotent state) and conventional primed hESCs (post-implantation epiblast-like), with this expression pattern maintained after 1 month of culture and requiring LIF for continued proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by appropriate citations characterizing the pluripotent states (Gafni et al., 2013; Kilens et al., 2018; Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016). Claims C35-C37 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1E-K, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, demonstrating reproducibility across cell lines and time points.

results.result: ACL treatment of H9-derived and SHEF6-derived hEPSCs, Rset hPSCs, and hESCs showed consistent upregulation of SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES and downregulation of SOX2 protein across all cell lines, though H9 hEPSCs showed SOX2 mRNA upregulation due to a GATA6-low/SOX2-high subpopulation, suggesting heterogeneous response.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, demonstrating reproducibility across multiple cell lines. The single-cell analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D provides evidence for the heterogeneous response interpretation in C42.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis using GSVA revealed that all three ACL-treated hPSC populations showed greater similarity to hypoblast than epiblast, with Rset-ACL most similar to hypoblast and hESC-ACL most similar to definitive endoderm.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1L showing GSVA analysis results. The methodology is described in the text and involves comparison to lineage-specific gene signatures from published datasets. The analysis appropriately uses sorted SOX17+ populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) to ensure purity.

results.result: The authors identified human-specific markers distinguishing extra-embryonic from definitive endoderm through differential gene expression analysis, finding 24,894 shared genes, 366 definitive endoderm-specific genes, and 1,250 extra-embryonic endoderm-specific genes including apolipoproteins (APOA1, APOA2, APOE, APOC1) and markers consistent with mouse extra-embryonic endoderm (PDGFRα, NID2, FN1, HNF1β, HNF4a, COL4A1, PITX2, PODXL).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by data in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2. Claims C50 and C52 are supported by Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2, with appropriate citations validating the markers (Baardman et al., 2013; Cindrova-Davies et al., 2017 for apolipoproteins; Ghatpande et al., 2002; Johansson et al., 1997; Kwon et al., 2008; Rodriguez et al., 2005; Shahbazi et al., 2017 for other markers). Claim C46 is supported by citation to Stern and Downs, 2012. This represents an important contribution identifying human-specific endoderm markers.

results.result: Using the newly identified markers, GSVA analysis revealed hESC-ACL is most similar to definitive endoderm, Rset-ACL is most similar to extra-embryonic endoderm (making them a candidate for modeling yolk sac), and hEPSC-ACL are intermediate (possibly due to heterogeneity), with the initial pluripotent state determining the endodermal fate induced by ACL treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2C. Claims C56-C59 represent reasonable interpretations of the data, with C57 supported by citation to Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019. The conclusion that pluripotent state determines endodermal fate (C56) is well-supported by the consistent pattern across multiple cell lines. Claims C58-C59 are reasonable hypotheses based on the data.

results.result: Analysis of BRACHYURY expression dynamics during ACL treatment showed that hESC-ACL and hEPSC-ACL populations exhibit a transient mesendoderm intermediate (BRACHYURY increase at day 2, decrease by day 4), while Rset hPSCs do not show this trend, indicating Rset hPSC specification dynamics are most similar to extra-embryonic endoderm specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by appropriate citations (Kimelman and Griffin, 2000; Niakan et al., 2012) establishing the developmental pathways. Claims C62-C63 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B tracking marker expression over 6 days. Claim C64 is a reasonable interpretation that Rset hPSCs follow an extra-embryonic endoderm-like developmental trajectory based on the absence of mesendoderm intermediate.

results.result: In human-mouse chimera experiments, both hEPSC-ACL and Rset-ACL contributed to mouse primitive endoderm (18% and 12% of chimeras respectively), with hEPSC-ACL showing some fate plasticity (3% contributing to both epiblast and primitive endoderm), contrasting with untreated hEPSCs and Rset hPSCs which predominantly contribute to epiblast, while primed hESC-ACL could not contribute to primitive endoderm.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2-3. The chimera methodology is clearly described, appropriate controls are included (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing ACL medium doesn't affect mouse embryo development), and quantification is provided. The functional validation through chimera contribution provides strong evidence for extra-embryonic endoderm identity.

results.result: Based on transcriptional and functional evidence, the authors conclude that Rset-ACL are most similar to human extra-embryonic endoderm and the most promising candidate for modeling human yolk sac, while hEPSC-ACL show mixed characteristics (likely due to heterogeneity) and hESC-ACL are more similar to definitive endoderm.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 represent reasonable conclusions drawn from the combined transcriptional profiling (Figure 1L, 2C) and functional chimera data (Figure 3D-F). The interpretation that Rset-ACL are the best candidate for yolk sac modeling is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence. Claims C72 is presented as a hypothesis to explain hEPSC-ACL heterogeneity, which is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Differential gene expression analysis between pre-implantation (E6-7) and post-implantation (E10-14) extra-embryonic endoderm identified 25,496 shared genes, 397 pre-implantation-specific genes, and 617 post-implantation-specific genes, including AXL (a mouse visceral endoderm marker) and apolipoproteins (APOA2, APOB) among post-implantation markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by data in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3. Claim C78 is supported by Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3 with citation to McDonald et al., 2014 validating AXL as a mouse marker. Claim C79 is a reasonable interpretation connecting to the yolk sac's role in apolipoprotein synthesis. This analysis provides important temporal markers for extra-embryonic endoderm development.

results.result: GSVA analysis comparing pre- vs. post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm markers revealed that Rset-ACL are most similar to post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm while T2iLGö-PrE are more similar to pre-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm, indicating Rset-ACL are the best candidate for modeling yolk sac-epiblast interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C using the markers identified in the previous analysis. Claim C82 is a reasonable conclusion that Rset-ACL, being most similar to post-implantation yolk sac, are appropriate for modeling post-implantation yolk sac-epiblast interactions. The comparison to T2iLGö-PrE provides important context showing that pluripotent state influences developmental stage of derived endoderm.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that the mouse AVE secretes BMP, WNT, and NODAL inhibitors to create signaling gradients determining anterior-posterior axis, that primate post-implantation hypoblast expresses similar inhibitors (DKK1, CER1, NOG), and that studies suggest an anterior hypoblast subpopulation may influence BMP signaling in human epiblast, implying the human yolk sac may harbor AVE-like cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by appropriate citations establishing mouse AVE function (Arnold and Robertson, 2009). Claims C86-C87 are supported by citations to studies of primate embryos (Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2016). Claim C88 is a reasonable inference based on the expression of signaling inhibitors in human hypoblast. This establishes the rationale for investigating whether YSLCs have AVE-like function.

results.result: Analysis of published datasets revealed that DKK1, CER1, LEFTY2, and SFRP1 are expressed at greater levels in post-implantation relative to pre-implantation hypoblast, while NOG is higher in pre-implantation hypoblast, and all analyzed inhibitors were upregulated in YSLCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by data in Figure 5A using published datasets (Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019). Claim C91 is supported by Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B showing expression in YSLCs. This provides important evidence that YSLCs express signaling inhibitors characteristic of post-implantation hypoblast/AVE.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that DKK1 and NOG act as WNT and BMP inhibitors in human stem cell models, CER1 antagonizes both NODAL and BMP signaling, and hypothesizes that YSLCs may share functional characteristics with mouse AVE and human anterior hypoblast in governing cell fate via BMP and WNT inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by appropriate citations (Martyn et al., 2019; Simunovic et al., 2019; Aykul and Martinez-Hackert, 2016) establishing the functions of these inhibitors. Claim C94 is a reasonable hypothesis based on the expression of these inhibitors in YSLCs. This sets up the functional experiments testing YSLC effects on hESCs.

results.result: The authors establish that hESCs lose pluripotent character (SOX2 expression) in a BMP-dependent manner when cultured in 3D Geltrex, and that inhibiting WNT signaling (with IWR1 or XAV) prevents SOX2 downregulation, indicating hESCs lose SOX2 in 3D Geltrex in response to BMP and WNT pathway activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by citation to Shao et al., 2017b. Claims C96-C97 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D confirming and extending previous findings. Claim C98 is a reasonable conclusion from the combined BMP and WNT inhibition experiments. This establishes the experimental system for testing YSLC effects.

results.result: Co-culture experiments showed that YSLCs cultured with hESCs at 1:1 ratio resulted in higher SOX2 levels and a slight (non-significant) increase in epithelial spheroids relative to disorganized structures, demonstrating YSLCs can inhibit SOX2 loss that would otherwise occur in 3D Geltrex.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-G. Claim C101 is a reasonable conclusion from the co-culture data. However, the effect is modest and the increase in epithelial spheroids is not statistically significant, suggesting the co-culture system has limitations (addressed in subsequent conditioned medium experiments).

results.result: YSLC-conditioned medium blocked SOX2 downregulation and significantly supported columnar epithelial morphology in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex, demonstrating YSLCs prevent SOX2 downregulation and support columnar spheroid formation via secreted components, though the effect is limited in physical co-culture likely due to reduced YSLC viability in 3D Geltrex.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5C-E showing significant effects of conditioned medium. Claim C104 is a well-supported conclusion from the conditioned medium experiments. Claim C105 is a reasonable hypothesis explaining why conditioned medium is more effective than co-culture. The conditioned medium approach provides cleaner evidence for secreted factor effects.

results.result: Analysis of downstream effectors revealed that both WNT (LEF1) and BMP (pSMAD1/5) pathways were active in control conditions but their activity decreased in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium in 3D hESC spheroids.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5F-H showing quantification of LEF1 and pSMAD1/5 levels. This provides direct evidence that YSLCs inhibit both WNT and BMP signaling pathways, supporting the proposed mechanism of action.

results.result: Addition of BMP4 to hESCs led to decreased SOX2 and increased pSMAD1/5, but YSLC conditioned medium prevented these changes; similarly, WNT3a treatment caused SOX2 loss and LEF1 upregulation, but YSLC conditioned medium significantly counteracted these effects, with similar trends observed for NANOG.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5I-L showing effects of BMP4 and WNT3a with and without YSLC conditioned medium. Claim C112 is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-K. These experiments provide strong evidence that YSLCs antagonize both BMP and WNT signaling through secreted factors, using controlled addition of pathway activators.

results.result: The authors conclude that YSLCs block loss of pluripotent gene expression by antagonizing WNT and BMP signaling via secreted factors and can thereby influence hESC fate.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is a well-supported conclusion from the combined evidence of conditioned medium experiments (C102-C103), pathway activity analysis (C106-C107), and pathway-specific inhibition experiments (C108-C112). Multiple complementary approaches converge on this conclusion.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that the mouse AVE induces anterior fate and represses primitive streak formation, that a similar function has been proposed for human anterior hypoblast, and hypothesizes that YSLCs may bear similarity to both and may prevent hESCs from differentiating into posterior epiblast fates.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by appropriate citations (Rivera-Pérez and Hadjantonakis, 2015; Molè et al., 2021). Claim C116 is a reasonable hypothesis based on YSLCs' ability to inhibit BMP and WNT signaling. This sets up experiments testing whether YSLCs can inhibit posterior fate specification.

results.result: In hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex, BRACHYURY was not induced while GATA6 was upregulated in control conditions, and GATA6 upregulation was blocked in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6A-C. This provides evidence that YSLCs can block posterior marker (GATA6) upregulation in 3D culture conditions.

results.result: In a 2D mesoderm induction protocol using BMP4, YSLC conditioned medium suppressed BRACHYURY upregulation while preventing SOX2 loss, also countered GATA6 upregulation, and suppressed posterior markers (EOMES, SOX17, MIXL1, FOXA2, GSC) at the RNA level, demonstrating YSLCs can inhibit posterior epiblast marker expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6D-G, with appropriate citation to the mesoderm induction protocol (Richter et al., 2014). Claim C122 is a well-supported conclusion from the combined 3D and 2D experiments. The use of both 3D and 2D systems strengthens the evidence for YSLC effects on posterior fate specification.

results.result: Time-course analysis of hESCs in YSLC conditioned medium in 3D showed higher OCT4 and NANOG at all timepoints, significantly different SOX2 from day 3, SOX1 steadily increasing over 5 days (but downregulated by day 7), OTX2 peaking at day 4, with co-expression of pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers, demonstrating YSLCs can upregulate pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers in 3D.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7A-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C showing detailed time-course analysis with appropriate statistical testing. Claim C128 is a well-supported conclusion from the time-course data. The temporal dynamics provide important insights into how YSLCs influence hESC fate.

results.result: Using YSLC conditioned medium in a 15-day neural differentiation protocol resulted in significant upregulation of anterior ectoderm markers (SOX1, PAX6, NESTIN, NOTCH1), with SOX2 downregulated but still present (as observed in early neural specification), and YSLC conditioned medium induced intermediate levels of anterior ectoderm markers relative to dual SMAD inhibition and control.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7F-H, with C130 supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018 validating the SOX2 expression pattern. Claim C131 is supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D. The neural differentiation experiments provide functional validation that YSLCs can promote anterior ectoderm fate, though the intermediate levels suggest YSLCs may not fully recapitulate dual SMAD inhibition.

results.result: The authors conclude that YSLCs support anterior ectoderm marker expression in combination with pluripotency markers and therefore share functional similarities with the mammalian AVE.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 represent well-supported conclusions from the combined evidence showing YSLCs: (1) express signaling inhibitors characteristic of AVE (C89-C91), (2) inhibit BMP and WNT signaling (C106-C112), (3) block posterior fate specification (C117-C122), and (4) promote anterior ectoderm markers while maintaining pluripotency markers (C123-C131). Multiple lines of evidence converge on functional similarity to AVE.
